tagline: Coastal miles link a working lighthouse, an inlet fort and a film-studio town.
intro: A1A’s Scenic & Historic Coastal Byway runs for 72 miles through St. Johns and Flagler counties, mostly on two-lane roadway. The drive links Atlantic beaches, estuaries and preserves, weaving through St. Augustine on the way south. Named an All-American Road in 2021, it is promoted by Friends of A1A for its nature, culture, archaeology and history. An archived Federal Highway Administration guide allows two hours for the drive.

At Summer Haven, road access began in the 1920s; before that, travelers came by boat or along the beach. The A1A name came from a 1946 decision to distinguish the coastal state road from parallel U.S. 1. Repeated storm washouts led to A1A’s relocation inland in the 1970s, leaving the old alignment as a county road. The scenic corridor later emerged from three Florida Scenic Highways established in the late 1990s: Ocean Shore, River to Sea Trail, and Scenic and Historic A1A.

Southbound from the St. Johns–Duval county line, pass through Ponte Vedra Beach toward St. Augustine. The Bridge of Lions carries A1A across Matanzas Bay to Anastasia Island. Continue south past Fort Matanzas, Summer Haven and Marineland to Flagler Beach, where Gamble Rogers Memorial State Recreation Area lies between the ocean and the Intracoastal Waterway.

moments.title: St. Augustine Light
moments.text: The working lighthouse at Anastasia Island’s north end is a replacement, built as erosion threatened its predecessor. Keeper William Russell lit the new tower in October 1874; he was the only keeper to serve in both. The old tower fell into the sea in 1880, and its ruins are now a submerged archaeological site. The present light retains its original Fresnel lens, restored after rifle fire broke 19 prisms in 1986. The Junior Service League championed that repair when the Coast Guard considered replacing the damaged lens with a modern beacon.
moments.notice: The light station includes the 1874 tower and the 1876 keepers’ house.

moments.title: Fort Matanzas
moments.text: This coquina tower on Rattlesnake Island guarded a water approach that bypassed St. Augustine’s main defenses. In 1740, Georgia governor James Oglethorpe used Matanzas Inlet to blockade the city during a 39-day siege. Spanish governor Manuel de Montiano then ordered the fort built; convicts, enslaved people and troops from Cuba supplied the construction labor. Completed in 1742, the shellstone structure rested on a foundation of pine pilings in marshy ground. It later deteriorated into a ruin, until the War Department began restoration in 1916 and repaired three vertical wall fissures by 1924.
moments.notice: The restored tower is built of coquina, a local shellstone.

moments.title: Marineland
moments.text: Marine Studios opened in June 1938 with a particular audience in mind: Hollywood filmmakers who needed underwater footage for movies and newsreels. The facility also welcomed the general public, allowing visitors to see marine life up close. Two years later, Marineland incorporated as a municipality. The marine park and the town share a name, but the town has its own government and extends into both Flagler and St. Johns counties. It sits within the Guana Tolomato Matanzas National Estuarine Research Reserve, where research and conservation now form part of the town’s identity.

moments.title: Gamble Rogers Memorial State Recreation Area
moments.text: At Flagler Beach, this park occupies land between the Atlantic Ocean and the Intracoastal Waterway. Its name honors Gamble Rogers, the Florida musician and storyteller whose songs returned to characters in a fictional county. By the 1970s, he performed regularly at the Florida Folk Festival, often as its headliner. Rogers was camping here on October 10, 1991, when a child asked him to help her father in the surf. He took an air mattress into the ocean to attempt a rescue; both men drowned. The Florida Legislature renamed the state park in his honor.
